summary:
The name ASTRIX is inspired by two words: Astronomy and Matrix. Astronomy represents our connection to space and satellite technology, while Matrix represents the interconnected system of data that helps us understand complex patterns.
ASTRIX is a project developed for NASA Space Apps
Challenge 2026, focusing on the harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS active fire data. Our goal is to bring observations from these two satellite sensors together into one interactive platform, making fire activity easier to explore, compare, and understand over time.
Through interactive maps, historical timelines, and data visualizations, ASTRIX aims to turn complex satellite observations into meaningful information that can support researchers, environmental organizations, and communities in understanding fire activity and its impact on people, wildlife, and the environment.
Our vision is simple: connect space data with real world environmental awareness
details:
ASTRIX is a web-based fire activity exploration platform that brings historical MODIS and VIIRS satellite active-fire observations into a more consistent monthly record. Through its interactive web application, Burn Calendar, users can explore where thermal hotspots were detected, identify periods of unusually high activity, compare historical patterns and understand how fire activity has changed over time.

The project aims to make complex satellite observations easier to access, interpret and use for environmental monitoring, research and decision-making.

### The Problem

Satellites have been recording active-fire hotspots across the Earth for more than two decades. However, MODIS and VIIRS instruments do not observe the Earth in exactly the same way. They differ in spatial resolution, detection sensitivity and observation schedules. As a result, their hotspot counts cannot simply be combined and treated as one continuous historical record.

A change in satellite instrument may create apparent changes in hotspot counts even when actual fire activity has not changed. This makes it difficult for researchers, fire managers and land managers to make fair comparisons across different periods.

### What ASTRIX Does

ASTRIX addresses this challenge through two connected components: a satellite-data harmonization workflow and an interactive web application called Burn Calendar.

The harmonization workflow processes monthly active-fire summaries from NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS observations. It applies filtering, spatial aggregation, observing-time adjustments and statistical calibration to make the records more comparable.

The Burn Calendar application then presents the processed information through an interactive global map, regional calendars, historical comparisons and downloadable datasets.

### How the Platform Works

The current prototype allows users to:

- Explore a global map and access the California example calendar.
- View monthly hotspot patterns across different years, with darker calendar cells representing higher detection counts.
- Compare selected months against historical medians.
- Explore percentage changes and percentile-based calendar visualizations.
- Select a geographic area by drawing a bounding box or entering coordinates within the dataset's coverage.
- Choose a date range and a reference period for historical comparison.
- Download monthly time series, year-by-month matrices and 0.25° grid-cell monthly aggregates in CSV format.

These features allow users to explore both regional and historical patterns without having to manually process large satellite datasets.

### NASA Data Sources and Processing

ASTRIX uses NASA FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System) active-fire products, including:

- MODIS observations from NASA's Terra and Aqua satellites.
- 375-metre VIIRS observations from Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21.

According to the platform's documented workflow, low-confidence detections and selected non-fire sources, such as volcanoes, gas flares and offshore sources, are filtered out.

The remaining detections are grouped into 0.25° geographic grid cells and monthly periods. The workflow also adjusts for changes in satellite observing time so that the addition of another observing satellite is not automatically interpreted as an increase in fire activity.

### MODIS–VIIRS Harmonization

One of the main technical components of ASTRIX is its harmonization approach.

Because MODIS and VIIRS have different observation characteristics, the platform uses their overlapping observation period from 2012 to 2019 to develop a statistical calibration.

The documented method adjusts MODIS counts towards the VIIRS scale using ratios calculated by 5° geographic tile and calendar month. Where observations are limited, the calibration pulls local ratios towards a global ratio to reduce the effect of sparse data.

The current historical record uses calibrated MODIS estimates through January 2012 and observed VIIRS data from February 2012 onward.

The team also describes testing the calibration using held-out overlap years, predicting VIIRS counts from MODIS observations and measuring the differences between the predicted and observed values.

This approach aims to make long-term fire activity patterns easier to compare while acknowledging that the two satellite instruments are not identical.

### What Makes ASTRIX Creative and Innovative?

The creativity of ASTRIX lies in combining satellite-data harmonization with an interactive calendar-based visualization.

Instead of presenting MODIS and VIIRS as separate datasets or requiring users to interpret complicated raw satellite records, ASTRIX brings the observations into a more consistent monthly timeline.

The Burn Calendar provides a different way to explore satellite fire information by combining geographic exploration, historical comparisons, monthly activity patterns and downloadable summaries in one platform.

It transforms complex satellite observations into a more accessible tool that can be explored by users with different levels of technical experience.

### Benefits and Intended Impact

ASTRIX aims to make historical satellite fire information more accessible, understandable and useful.

Its potential benefits include:

- Helping researchers identify seasonal fire activity and long-term patterns.
- Supporting fire-management and emergency-response teams in understanding historical activity.
- Helping land managers and conservation groups identify areas that may require closer monitoring or further investigation.
- Allowing users to compare current observations with historical conditions.
- Reducing the time and technical effort needed to process and compare separate satellite datasets.
- Supporting environmental education and research through accessible data visualization.

In the longer term, ASTRIX aims to contribute to improved environmental monitoring, more informed planning and better understanding of fire activity across different regions.

### Intended Users

ASTRIX is designed for users who need to understand fire activity across different locations and time periods, including:

- Environmental and fire researchers.
- Early-warning and emergency-response teams.
- Land and forest managers.
- Conservation and wildlife organizations.
- Government and environmental agencies.
- Universities and educational institutions.

The platform is intended as a decision-support and exploration tool that can help users identify patterns and determine where further investigation may be useful.

### Tools and Technologies Used

The project combines NASA satellite data, data-processing methods and web-based visualization.

The tools and resources identified in the current project include:

- **NASA FIRMS:** Primary source of MODIS and VIIRS active-fire observations.
- **MODIS and VIIRS:** Satellite instruments providing the active-fire observations used in the project.
- **GitHub:** Used to host and manage the project's source-code repository.
- **GitHub Pages:** Used to publish the web-based prototype.
- **CSV data outputs:** Used to provide downloadable monthly summaries and aggregated datasets.
- **Burn Calendar:** The interactive web application developed to visualize and explore the harmonized fire activity records.

The processing workflow includes statistical calibration, filtering, geographic aggregation and observing-time adjustments. The current prototype is primarily data-driven and uses statistical harmonization rather than claiming to use a machine-learning model.

The specific programming languages, frameworks and libraries used in the source code have not been confirmed, so they are not listed here. The current prototype is web-based and does not require dedicated physical hardware.

### Factors Considered During Development

The team considered several important factors while developing ASTRIX:

1. **Satellite differences:** MODIS and VIIRS have different spatial resolutions, sensitivities and observation schedules.
2. **Data reliability:** Low-confidence detections and selected non-fire sources need to be filtered.
3. **Historical consistency:** Changes in satellite coverage and observing time should not automatically be interpreted as changes in fire activity.
4. **Calibration uncertainty:** Statistical harmonization improves comparability but cannot make the two instruments identical.
5. **Geographic coverage:** Users should be able to explore different regions and select areas of interest.
6. **Accessibility and usability:** Complex satellite information should be presented through a simple, interactive interface.
7. **Practical usefulness:** Users should be able to compare historical periods and download summarized information for further analysis.
8. **Responsible interpretation:** The platform should communicate the limitations of satellite hotspot observations and avoid presenting them as confirmed fires.

### Potential Contribution

ASTRIX does not aim to create a new satellite or replace NASA's existing data services. Its contribution is to make two important satellite observation records more usable together through a consistent historical view.

By combining harmonized monthly records, regional comparisons and downloadable summaries, the project can make satellite fire information more accessible to users who may not have the time or technical resources to process raw datasets themselves.

### Current Scope and Limitations

ASTRIX is currently a decision-support and data-exploration prototype, not an operational fire alarm or a replacement for official emergency information.

A satellite hotspot represents a detected thermal anomaly. It does not necessarily confirm an active wildfire, identify the cause of the heat or measure the actual area burned. Detections can also be affected by cloud cover, satellite overpass timing and sensor characteristics.

The platform's downloadable CSV files contain monthly 0.25° aggregated data rather than individual hotspot detections. Users who require raw point-level observations should obtain them directly from NASA FIRMS.

Additionally, pre-2012 values in the calendar are calibrated estimates rather than direct VIIRS observations. These distinctions are important when interpreting historical comparisons.

### Next Steps

The team plans to continue validating the harmonization method against overlapping MODIS and VIIRS observations, document the calibration method and its uncertainty, and test the interface with potential users.

Future improvements may include expanding regional coverage and use cases, improving data-quality indicators, and gathering feedback from researchers and fire-management practitioners to identify which comparisons and downloadable outputs would be most useful.

Ultimately, ASTRIX aims to turn complex satellite observations into a clearer picture of fire activity over time, helping people better understand the past and make more informed decisions for the future.

### Team Composition

ASTRIX was developed by a multidisciplinary team consisting of two IT students, one business student and one business graduate. The team combines technical and business perspectives to develop a solution that addresses a real environmental data challenge.

ASTRIX is a web-based fire activity platform that combines historical MODIS and VIIRS satellite observations into a more consistent monthly record. Through its interactive application, Burn Calendar, users can explore fire activity across different regions, compare monthly hotspot counts with historical medians, identify unusual patterns and download summarized data.

The project addresses a challenge in satellite fire monitoring: MODIS and VIIRS have different spatial resolutions, detection sensitivities and observation schedules, making their hotspot counts difficult to compare directly. ASTRIX aims to reduce these differences through a statistical harmonization workflow.

The platform uses NASA FIRMS active-fire data from MODIS Terra and Aqua, and 375-metre VIIRS observations from Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21. Its processing workflow removes low-confidence detections and selected non-fire sources, groups observations into 0.25° grid cells by month and satellite, adjusts for satellite observing effort, and calibrates MODIS towards the VIIRS scale using their overlapping observation period from 2012 to 2019. The historical record uses calibrated MODIS through January 2012 and observed VIIRS from February 2012 onward. The calibration is tested using held-out overlap years.

The current prototype includes three regions: California, Mesopotamia and Australia. It allows users to select a region, draw a geographic area, choose a date range, explore year-by-month calendars, compare activity against historical medians, view percentage changes and percentile-based colours, and download monthly time series, year-by-month matrices and 0.25° grid-cell summaries as CSV files. The platform also includes interactive colour indicators, hover values and a table view.

The team's dataset contains approximately 46.4 million FIRMS detections, of which 38.2 million were retained after filtering. The reported validation indicators include a 0.98 year-to-year match for the Terra and Aqua era (2002–2012), an 11% total miss during the same period, and a 0.97 Terra-only match for 2000–2002, with a 17% miss. These are project-specific validation measures, not wildfire prediction accuracy.

ASTRIX is creative because it combines satellite-data harmonization with an interactive calendar, making complex historical observations easier to explore and compare. Rather than replacing NASA FIRMS, it builds on NASA's data to provide a more consistent historical view. Its potential users include environmental researchers, fire-management teams, land managers, conservation groups and educational institutions. The platform could help identify seasonal patterns, compare current activity with historical conditions and highlight areas that may need further investigation.

The project uses NASA FIRMS data, statistical processing, CSV outputs, GitHub for source-code management and GitHub Pages to publish the web application. The specific programming languages and libraries have not yet been confirmed. The current prototype is web-based and does not require dedicated physical hardware.

During development, the team considered satellite differences, data quality, observation effort, calibration reliability, geographic coverage, accessibility, usability and responsible interpretation of hotspot data. A hotspot represents a detected thermal anomaly, not necessarily a confirmed wildfire or the actual area burned. Cloud cover, satellite timing and sensor characteristics can also affect detections.

ASTRIX is currently a decision support and exploration prototype, not an operational fire alarm. Only three regions are currently available, pre-2012 values are calibrated estimates, and the downloadable CSV files contain monthly aggregates rather than individual detections. Future improvements include expanding coverage towards the whole globe, adding downloadable individual detections, integrating live NASA FIRMS updates, checking colour accessibility and continuing to validate the harmonization method.

The project was developed by a four-member multidisciplinary team. Alaa Al Jahdami leads the vision, strategy and partnerships as CEO and co-founder; Al Munther Al Harrasi leads the technical direction; Mundhir Ali develops the software and works with AI tools; and Saba Alhinai leads market research, pilot opportunities and finance. The team also shared responsibilities across development, design, video editing, research, brainstorming and coordination.

ASTRIX aims to turn complex satellite observations into a clearer picture of fire activity over time, supporting more accessible environmental monitoring and informed decision-making.

Two satellites. One timeline. A clearer picture of fire.
